Empirical Research Plan – Schooling and Earnings (NLSYM)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Strategy: Two–Stage Least Squares (Instrumental‐Variables, IV)

Why IV?  
• The parameter of interest is the causal return to an additional year of schooling (a continuous, choice variable).  
• Schooling is endogenous because high-ability or better-connected youths both acquire more education and earn higher wages.  
• The data contain a plausibly exogenous source of variation – whether the young man grew up in a county that had (in 1966) at least one four-year college (“college proximity”).  
• This geographic variation affects the cost of attending college but should not directly influence wages in the mid-1970s once we control for individual and regional observables.  
Hence 2SLS using college-proximity as the instrument is appropriate.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
Sᵢ  = completed years of schooling of individual i (measured by 1976).

Instrument (binary):  
Zᵢ = 1 if respondent’s 1966 county contained ≥1 accredited 4-year college  
Zᵢ = 0 otherwise

Control group / counterfactual:  
Individuals who did not grow up in a county with a 4-year college.

Treatment timing:  
Proximity is predetermined (measured when the respondent was 14-24 in 1966) and precedes both completed schooling (late 1960s / early 1970s) and earnings (1976). No staggered timing issues.

(If desired we could refine Zᵢ to a continuous “distance to nearest college” or the number of colleges within X miles; the core logic is identical.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Relevance – Growing up near a college increases completed schooling.  
Plausibility: Historically, college attendance rates were highly sensitive to travel distance; previous descriptive work shows ~0.2–0.4 extra years of schooling for those with nearby colleges.

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on controls, college proximity affects 1976 wages only through schooling.  
Plausibility: Reasonable because respondents typically left their home county by 1976 and labor markets are national. Unobserved county characteristics (e.g., quality of K-12 schools, local networks) threaten this assumption but can be mitigated with rich controls and regional fixed effects.

A3. Independence (Ignorability) – College locations were not strategically placed in counties with systematically higher-ability youths.  
Plausibility: College establishment long predates respondents’ births and often driven by historical or religious factors, not contemporaneous youth ability.

A4. Monotonicity – Nobody is less likely to attend school because a college is nearby (“no defiers”).  
Plausibility: Lower cost should weakly increase schooling.

A5. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA) – One individual’s schooling decision does not affect another’s wage within the sample in ways correlated with the instrument.  
Plausibility: Reasonable in a national cross-section of individuals.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Non-excludability via local labor-market demand  
   • Counties with colleges may have more high-wage employers in 1970s.  
Mitigation: Control for 1970 county characteristics (manufacturing share, population, median income); include state fixed effects; run robustness excluding individuals living in their home county in 1976.

T2. Sorting / selective migration of families toward college counties before 1966  
   • High-education parents might locate near colleges, violating independence.  
Mitigation: Control for parental education, parental income proxy, race; compare observable pre-treatment characteristics; perform balance tests; re-estimate on subsample of families residing in the same county since child’s birth (if available).

T3. Weak instrument risk  
   • Limited first-stage strength reduces precision and can bias 2SLS in small samples.  
Mitigation: Report first-stage F-statistic (rule-of-thumb >10); try alternative, continuous distance measures to improve strength; cluster SEs at county level.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Load packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)      # fast 2SLS
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Data loading -------------------------------------------------------------
nls <- read_csv("NLSYM_1966_1976.csv")  # hypothetical file

# 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------------------
analysis <- nls %>% 
  mutate(
    ln_wage76 = log(wage_1976_hourly),                # outcome
    schoolyrs = years_schooling_1976,                 # endogenous
    nearcollege = ifelse(college_in1966_county == 1, 1, 0), # instrument
    exper = age_1976 - schoolyrs - 6,                 # Mincer experience approx.
    black = (race == "Black"),
    south1966 = (region1966 == "South")
  ) %>% 
  drop_na(ln_wage76, schoolyrs, nearcollege, exper, age_1976)

# 3. Main 2SLS regression ------------------------------------------------------
# First stage strength check
fs <- feols(schoolyrs ~ nearcollege + black + exper + I(exper^2) +
              south1966 + parental_ed_mother + parental_ed_father |
              state1966, data = analysis, cluster = "county1966")
summary(fs)

# Second stage (2SLS)
iv_main <- feols(ln_wage76 ~ 1 | schoolyrs ~ nearcollege |
                   black + exper + I(exper^2) + south1966 +
                   parental_ed_mother + parental_ed_father |
                   state1966, data = analysis, cluster = "county1966")
etable(fs, iv_main, tex = FALSE)

# 4. Robustness check: using distance (continuous IV) -------------------------
analysis <- analysis %>% 
  mutate(dist_nearest = distance_to_nearest_college_miles)

iv_dist <- feols(ln_wage76 ~ 1 | schoolyrs ~ dist_nearest |
                   black + exper + I(exper^2) + south1966 |
                   state1966, data = analysis, cluster = "county1966")

# Robustness check 2: Drop men living in home county in 1976
iv_movers <- feols(ln_wage76 ~ 1 | schoolyrs ~ nearcollege |
                     black + exper + I(exper^2) + south1966 |
                     state1966,
                   data = filter(analysis, stayed_in_home_county == 0),
                   cluster = "county1966")

modelsummary(list(iv_main, iv_dist, iv_movers),
             gof_omit = 'Adj|Within|F', stars = TRUE)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (human-capital) predicts a positive causal return.  
Historical evidence for the 1960s-70s U.S. men: roughly 7–10 % higher hourly wage per additional year of schooling. Expect 2SLS estimate to lie in that range or slightly above OLS (OLS tends to be downward-biased if ability is positively correlated but fixed, yet upward-biased if ability drives both schooling and wages; the 1960s literature usually finds IV ≥ OLS).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) ..................... 1  
C2: Instrument excludability (no direct wage effect) ............ 0.8  
C3: Independence / balance on observables ....................... 0.8  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) .................................. 1  
C5: SUTVA (no interference) .................................... 1  

Average score ≈ 0.92 — credible but excludability and independence
warrant extensive robustness and discussion.
